description: The portfolio's Renovate configuration, extended by name rather than copied: `"extends": ["github>youndie/sborka"]`.

It was not designed here. Ten repositories had written the same file — the same timezone, the same Monday schedule, the same four groups in the same order — and the five that had not written it are where the defects are: konekt took one sborka release as two pull requests (#5 and #7 for 0.2.0.30), because the rule that says a release is one thing lives in the ten files and not in the five.

What is NOT here is anything a repository has to decide for itself: automerge (see the `automerge-harness` preset next door and the precondition it names), which of its own images or charts to ignore, and every group that exists because of one repository's dependencies.

Note on merging: `packageRules` from a preset are concatenated with the repository's own, preset first, and the last matching rule wins. Every other array — `ignorePaths`, `labels` — is REPLACED by the repository's value, so a repository adding one ignore path has to repeat the two below.

packageRules.description: Kotlin: the compiler and its plugins move as one version, and that is never a routine bump.
kotlinx ships as one release train — one pull request.

description: kotlinx-datetime publishes `-compat` builds for consumers pinned to an older line: `0.8.0-0.6.x-compat` is not a newer version but 0.8.0 compiled against the OLD 0.6.x API. Such a build sorts as newer, Renovate reads it as an upgrade, and taking it moves a repository backwards.

ANY `-compat` suffix, not the 0.6.x line by name. This started as `!/-0\.6\.x-compat$/` — the line that existed — and five repositories were already refusing the whole shape locally: smtpkn, tracy, katcher, shildik and metrik. They were right, and the narrow pattern would have re-opened the next line the day it was published, silently. The rule is scoped to one package, so there is nothing else for the wider pattern to catch.

Six repositories had this guard and two did not, and both of those were being offered it while the preset was being written — konekt as an open pull request, petich on its dashboard. That is the argument for the preset in one line.

sborka is one release, not one release per place it is named. The settings plugin is applied in settings.gradle.kts and the conventions come from the catalog's version ref; they share a classloader, so a repository that moves one and not the other runs 0.2.x settings against 0.1.x conventions.

BOTH group names on purpose. The plugin ids moved to `io.github.youndie.sborka` in youndie/sborka#23 while every consumer still names `ru.workinprogress.sborka`, so a rule naming only the old one keeps working until the day a repository migrates — and then stops matching without saying anything, which is the same split coming back.

packageRules.description: The build harness arrives as one pull request, not one per action. Whether it may then merge itself is a separate question, and a separate preset.

description: sborka's actions and `publish-wip.yaml` are pinned to the tag every sborka publish writes, `v<X.Y.Z.N>` (youndie/sborka#123), and Renovate cannot read that tag on its own. Since 2026-04 the `github-actions` manager uses `github-actions` versioning, which strips the `v` and then asks for strict SemVer: `0.5.0.124` is not a version to it, so the next tag would never be offered.

Four numeric parts are what `regex` versioning's `build` group is for: compared after the patch and treated as a patch update. Scoped to the tag lookup (`github-tags`) so that a reference still on `@main`, which Renovate resolves as a digest, is not re-read as an invalid version.

packageRules.description: A major of anything that ships gets a human. `automerge-harness` deliberately overrides this for the harness, which ships to nobody.

description: THE STACK IS HELD until Kotlin 2.5.20: the compiler on 2.4.x, KSP on 2.3.x, Compose Multiplatform on 1.12.x, AGP on 9.4.x, Gradle on 9.8.x. Patches still arrive; a new line does not. This rule is the compiler; the four after it are the rest.

They move together or not at all. A Gradle that KGP has not been tested against, an AGP that asks for a newer Gradle, a Compose built against the next compiler: each is a pull request that is green in one repository and breaks the portfolio's agreement with itself. The portfolio was aligned on 2.4.20 / 2.3.12 / 1.12.1 / 9.4.1 on 2026-10-01, and moved to Gradle 9.8.0 on 2026-10-02 after its pull requests had been green in mani, kachok, chronik and telek.

Regexes rather than ranges on purpose: in Maven ordering `1.13.0-alpha01` sorts BELOW `1.13.0`, so `<1.13.0` would let the next line's prereleases through to anything already on a prerelease, and material3 is. One rule per package rather than one shared pattern, so that KSP cannot take 2.4.x by matching the compiler's line.
LIFTING IT is one deliberate change here when 2.5.20 is out: all five rules at once, not one package at a time.

description: Held with the compiler, see above. The line named here has to admit the `gradle` version in catalog/sborka.versions.toml, and `verifyGradleVersion` fails sborka's `check` when it does not: the catalog is where the version is decided, this rule only stops Renovate from proposing a different one.

BY DATASOURCE AND NAME, NOT BY MANAGER. Gradle reaches a repository twice: as the wrapper, and as the official `gradle:<version>-jdk25-noble` image a Dockerfile builds in — and the two are read by different managers. Matched by `matchManagers: ["gradle-wrapper"]`, this rule held the wrapper and let the image through: on 2026-10-02, with the wrapper held on 9.7.x, youndie/mostik's dependency dashboard was offering `gradle 9.7.1-jdk25-noble → 9.8.0-jdk25-noble` from its Dockerfile. `gradle-version` is the wrapper's datasource and `docker` is the image's wherever it is named — a Dockerfile, a compose file, a workflow's `container:` — and the name has to be exactly `gradle`, so no other image or artefact is caught. `verifyGradleVersion` finds the rule by this shape and fails if it goes back to matching one manager.
